Masterpiece of the week
Head of Christ Crucified by the Master of Liesborn (Johann von Soest?) , probably early 1480s-1490

blocks.alt: Head of Christ Crucified by the Master of Liesborn (Johann von Soest?), probably early 1480s-1490
blocks.caption: Photograph: The National Gallery, London

blocks.text: The blood streams over Christ’s deathly white face in a vivid, almost Hammer horror contrast between gore and pallor. It flows in thick rivulets from the crown of thorns that has been mockingly forced on to his head. The initials INRI on a piece of paper fixed to the cross stand for “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” in Latin, and the cruel crown rams home the barb. Christ bears the laughter and the physical pain with patience and dignity, lowering his eyes in sorrow as he waits for his earthly body to die. The stark, simple shock of this image comes from an age in which Europeans were encouraged to identify with Christ, to imagine themselves suffering alongside him. At the same time this artist’s explicit focus on flowing blood may serve a theological function: the central moment of the medieval Mass was the miraculous transformation of bread and wine into the actual body and blood of Christ. According to the philosopher Thomas Aquinas this took place literally: the bread and wine kept their “accidental” appearance while changing their “essential” nature. This painting is part of an altarpiece from Germany, but not all Germans were convinced by such ideas. In the early 1500s Martin Luther would rebel against the miracle of transubstantiation, and against art like this which he regarded as idolatry. National Gallery, London
